references.text: The same pattern of slaughter at the entrance to the tent of meeting and sprinkling of blood around the altar for the peace offering
Slaughter of the bull before the Lord at the tent of meeting, the same liturgical practice
The blood makes atonement on the altar, the theological basis for the sprinkling of blood
The blood is sprinkled around on the altar, a parallel practice during the consecration of the altar
Moses sprinkles blood on the altar at the making of the covenant, foundational for blood rituals
The role of the priests in sprinkling the blood on the altar is confirmed
The priests sprinkle the blood on the altar, a continuation of the Levitical practice
Hebrews explains that almost everything is cleansed with blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness
Blood from bulls and goats cannot take away sins, pointing forward to Christ's perfect sacrifice
Jesus' blood as the final atoning sacrifice, fulfillment of the Levitical blood sacrifices
Illustrates that the ritual for the sprinkling of blood is independent of the type of sacrificial animal (cattle or sheep), but maintains unity in the atonement process.
Confirms that the ritual for the guilt offering with a female lamb follows exactly the same principles regarding location and handling of blood as the burnt offering.
Shows that the ritual involving a goat as a guilt offering follows the same strict protocol for sprinkling of blood as other sacrificial animals.
Highlights the transition from the law's instruction to historical fulfillment when Aaron performed the sacrifice exactly as prescribed.
Creates a theological contrast between sprinkling on the altar of burnt offering (Lev 1) and pouring out the remaining blood at its base in the sin offering (Lev 4), while both occur at the entrance.
Highlights the difference in blood handling between the burnt offering (sprinkling around) and the sin offering for the community (smearing on the horns and pouring out), both at the entrance.
Connects the details of the sacrificial laws in Leviticus to their origin and consecration context in Exodus.
